facts.statement: The genus Titanis was described by Brodkorb in 1963.
facts.quote: authority: Brodkorb, 1963

facts.statement: The first fossils of Titanis were found by Benjamin Waller and Robert Allen in the Santa Fe River, Florida, and named Titanis walleri by Pierce Brodkorb in 1963.
facts.quote: The first fossils were unearthed by amateur paleontologists/archaeologists Benjamin Waller and Robert Allen from the Santa Fe River in Florida and were named Titanis walleri by ornithologist Pierce Brodkorb in 1963

facts.statement: The holotype of Titanis consists of an incomplete right tarsometatarsus and a phalanx.
facts.quote: The holotype material is fragmentary, consisting of only an incomplete right tarsometatarsus (lower leg bone) and phalanx (toe bone)

facts.statement: The earliest Titanis fossils were discovered in the winter of 1961/1962.
facts.quote: The earliest discovery of Titanis fossils occurred in the winter of 1961/1962

facts.statement: Titanis fossils have been found in five locations in Florida, including the Santa Fe River, Citrus County, Port Charlotte, Charlotte County, and a shell pit in Sarasota County.
facts.quote: Titanis has been found in five locales in Florida: Santa Fe River sites 1a and 1b and Inglis 1b, Citrus County; Port Charlotte, Charlotte County; and a shell pit in Sarasota County.

facts.statement: Out of 40 Titanis specimens found in Florida, 27 were recovered from the Santa Fe River.
facts.quote: Of the 40 Floridan specimens of Titanis, 27 have been unearthed from the Santa Fe River

facts.statement: A Titanis fossil was described in 1995 from a pit near Odem, Texas.
facts.quote: A newer discovery of Titanis was described in 1995; an isolated pedal phalanx that had been recovered from a sand and gravel pit near Odem along the Nueces River in San Patricio County, Texas.

facts.statement: G. Davidson Woodward collected avian fossils, including a wing bone and premaxilla, from the Olla Formation in California in 1961.
facts.quote: In 1961, while fossil collecting, G. Davidson Woodward acquired several avian fossils from sediments in the Pliocene-aged (3.7 million year old) strata of the Olla Formation in Anza-Borrego Desert State Park, California, including a wing bone found in association with the premaxilla of a giant bird.

facts.statement: In 2013, Robert Chandler and colleagues assigned a premaxilla from California to the genus Titanis.
facts.quote: a 2013 paper by paleontologist Robert Chandler and colleagues assigned the premaxilla to Titanis

facts.statement: Titanis lived from the Early Pliocene to the Early Pleistocene.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Early Pliocene-Early Pleistocene (Hemphillian-Blancan)~

facts.statement: The Florida Titanis fossils date to the Blancan stage, between 2.2 and 1.8 million years ago.
facts.quote: they originated from the upper part of the Blancan stage (2.2–1.8 million years old).

facts.statement: A Texas Titanis fossil is estimated to be 5 million years old, making it older than the Florida specimens.
facts.quote: This would make it the oldest estimate of a Titanis fossil at 5 million years old, compared to the Floridan fossils which are around 2.2–1.8 million years old, and therefore from the Blancan age.

facts.statement: The California Titanis premaxilla was originally estimated to be 3.5 to 3 million years old.
facts.quote: The age of the Anza-Borrego premaxilla was estimated at 3.5-3 mya based off the original estimates from the paper describing the material.

facts.statement: Detailed dating suggests the Olla Formation in California is between 4 and 2 million years old.
facts.quote: More detailed studies using magnetostratigraphy and tuff dating about the Olla Formation have indicated a middle-late Blancan age (4-2 mya) for the Olla Formation.

facts.statement: Recent estimates suggest Titanis stood 1.4 to 2 meters tall and weighed over 300 kg.
facts.quote: More recent estimates placed Titanis at 1.4 to 2 m in height and over 300 kg in body mass.

facts.statement: The skull of Titanis is estimated to be between 36 cm and 56 cm long.
facts.quote: The skull is estimated to have been between 36 cm and 56 cm in length, one of the largest known from any bird.

facts.statement: Titanis likely preyed on mammals such as Holmesina, Glyptotherium, equids, tapirs, and capybaras.
facts.quote: It likely preyed on mammals such as the extinct armadillo relatives Holmesina and Glyptotherium, equids, tapirs, capybaras, and other Pliocene herbivores.

facts.statement: Titanis is the only phorusrhacid known from North America.
facts.quote: Titanis is unique among phorusrhacids in that it is the only one known from North America, having evolved from phorusrhacids that island-hopped into North America millions of years before the Great American Interchange.

facts.statement: Titanis is a genus of phorusrhacid in the order Cariamiformes.
facts.quote: Titanis (meaning "Titan" for the Titans of Greek mythology) is a genus of phorusrhacid ("terror birds", a group originating in South America), an extinct family of large, predatory birds, in the order Cariamiformes

facts.statement: Titanis is classified in the subfamily Phorusrhacinae.
facts.quote: The species was classified in the subfamily Phorusrhacinae, which includes some of the last and largest phorusrhacids like Devincenzia and Kelenken.

facts.statement: Brodkorb grouped Titanis in the subfamily Phorusrhacinae within Phorusrhacidae.
facts.quote: As suggested by Ray, Brodkorb grouped Titanis with the subfamily Phorusrhacinae within Phorusrhacidae, along with Phorusrhacos and Devincenzia.

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding the classification of a California fossil, with some studies assigning it to Aiolornis and others to Titanis.
facts.quote: The wing bone was referred to the teratorn Aiolornis at that time, an assessment backed by ornithologist Hildegarde Howard in 1972. This was supported by later studies, but a 2013 paper by paleontologist Robert Chandler and colleagues assigned the premaxilla to Titanis

facts.statement: Titanis lived alongside placental mammalian predators such as Smilodon, Miracinonyx, Aenocyon, and Arctodus.
facts.quote: Titanis itself coexisted with a variety of placental mammalian predators, including carnivorans like the saber-toothed cat Smilodon, cheetah-like Miracinonyx, wolf-like Aenocyon, and the short-faced bear Arctodus.

facts.statement: Titanis is consistently classified within the subfamily Phorusrhacinae alongside Phorusrhacos, Kelenken, and Devincenzia.
facts.quote: Titanis, however, has consistently been regarded as being within the subfamily Phorusrhacinae along with Phorusrhacos, Kelenken, and Devincenzia.

facts.statement: A 2011 phylogenetic analysis by Alvarenga et al. placed Titanis in a polytomy rather than separating the subfamilies Brontornithinae, Phorusrhacinae, and Patagornithinae.
facts.quote: Brazilian paleontologist Herculano Alvarenga and colleagues published a phylogenetic analysis of Phorusrhacidae in 2011 that did not separate Brontornithinae, Phorusrhacinae, and Patagornithinae, resulting in Titanis in a polytomy (topology 1).

facts.statement: A 2015 analysis by Degrange et al. found the subfamily Phorusrhacinae to be polyphyletic, a finding that impacts Titanis's classification.
facts.quote: In their 2015 description of Llallawavis, the Argentinian paleontologist Federico J. Degrange and colleagues performed a phylogenetic analysis of Phorusrhacidae, wherein they found Phorusrhacinae to be polyphyletic, or an unnatural grouping (topology 2).

facts.statement: Titanis was very similar to the South American phorusrhacids Phorusrhacos and Devincenzia.
facts.quote: Overall, Titanis was very similar to the South American Phorusrhacos and Devincenzia, its closest relatives.

facts.statement: Accurate scaling estimates Titanis' total height at between 1.4 and 2 meters.
facts.quote: Accurate scaling after the discovery of new material estimated its total height around 1.4 to 2 m tall.

facts.statement: Weight estimates for Titanis vary, with a 1995 proposal suggesting 150 kg for a 2-meter tall individual and a 2005 study suggesting over 300 kg.
facts.quote: In 1995, Jon A. Baskin proposed that a 2 m tall individual would have weighed 150 kg, but the 2005 study which cited Baskin suggested it to be over 300 kg.

facts.statement: The preserved premaxilla of Titanis includes the frontmost end with a long, sharp beak tip used for hunting.
facts.quote: The premaxilla of Titanis is incomplete, consisting of its frontmost end including the characteristic long, sharp beak tip of Phorusrhacidae that would have been used for hunting.

facts.statement: The preserved premaxilla of Titanis measures 9 cm in length and 5.5 cm in height with a triangular vertical cross-section.
facts.quote: Its preserved length is 9 cm with a height of 5.5 cm with a triangular shape in vertical cross-section.

facts.statement: Two quadratojugals have been preserved in Titanis, and they exhibit different anatomies.
facts.quote: Two quadratojugals are preserved, both with different anatomies.

facts.statement: A partial mandible of Titanis is known but has not been figured or described in scientific literature.
facts.quote: In the lower jaw, a partial mandible is known but it is unfigured and undescribed in scientific literature.

facts.statement: Titanis is distinguished from other phorusrhacines by the distal end of its tarsometatarsus mid-trochlea being spread out onto its sides.
facts.quote: Titanis is distinguished from other phorusrhacines by the anatomy of its tarsometatarsus; the distal end of the mid-trochlea is spread out onto its sides.

facts.statement: Titanis had a large foot with three digits, the third of which possessed an enlarged claw similar to dromaeosaurid dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The pes is large and had three digits, the third of which had an enlarged ungual akin to that of dromaeosaurid dinosaurs.

facts.statement: The sickle claw of Titanis walleri was 8 cm in length.
facts.quote: The second toe bone or sickle claw of T. walleri was 8 cm in length.

facts.statement: Titanis co-existed with large carnivorous borhyaenid mammals for much of its existence.
facts.quote: They co-existed with some large, carnivorous borhyaenid mammals for much of their existence.

facts.statement: Researchers Alvarenga and Elizabeth Höfling discussed phorusrhacid habits in a 2003 article.
facts.quote: Alvarenga and Elizabeth Höfling made some general remarks about phorusrhacid habits in a 2003 article.

facts.statement: Titanis was flightless, a trait evidenced by the proportional size of its wings and body mass.
facts.quote: They were flightless, as evidenced by the proportional size of their wings and body mass, and the wing-size was more reduced in larger members of the group.

facts.statement: Titanis likely hunted by sight in open, sunlit areas rather than shaded forests, supported by large lacrimal bone expansions that protected its eyes.
facts.quote: The large expansions above the eyes formed by the lacrimal bones (similar to what is seen in modern hawks) would have protected the eyes against the sun, and enabled keen eyesight, which indicates they hunted by sight in open, sunlit areas, and not shaded forests.

facts.statement: In 2005, Rudemar Ernesto Blanco and Washington W. Jones examined the tibiotarsus strength of phorusrhacids to estimate speed, though they noted such estimates are unreliable.
facts.quote: In 2005, Rudemar Ernesto Blanco and Washington W. Jones examined the strength of the tibiotarsus (shin bone) of phorusrhacids to determine their speed, but conceded that such estimates can be unreliable even for extant animals.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested Titanis used its leg strength to break the long bones of medium-sized mammals like saigas or Thomson's gazelles rather than for high-speed running.
facts.quote: They found these estimates unlikely due to the large body size of these birds, and instead suggested the strength could have been used to break the long-bones of medium-sized mammals, the size for example of a saiga or Thomson's gazelle.

facts.statement: Titanis likely used its legs as kicking weapons to access marrow or defend itself, consistent with its large, curved, sideways-compressed claws.
facts.quote: This strength could be used for accessing the marrow inside the bones, or by using the legs as kicking weapons (like some modern ground birds do), consistent with the large, curved, and sideways compressed claws known in some phorusrhacids.

facts.statement: In 2006, Luis Chiappe suggested that Kelenken, similar to Titanis, was as fast as a greyhound and that grazing mammals provided ample prey despite other large predators.
facts.quote: In a 2006 news article, Luis Chiappe, an Argentine paleontologist, stated that Kelenken, a similar genus to Titanis, would have been as quick as a greyhound, and that while there were other large predators in South America at the time, they were limited in numbers and not as fast and agile as the phorusrhacids, and the many grazing mammals would have provided ample prey.

facts.statement: Luis Chiappe noted that phorusrhacids resembled predatory dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurus due to their gigantic heads, small forelimbs, and long legs.
facts.quote: Chiappe remarked that phorusrhacids crudely resembled earlier predatory dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurus, in having gigantic heads, very small forelimbs, and very long legs, and thereby similar carnivore adaptations.

facts.statement: A 2010 study by Degrange and colleagues used finite element analysis and CT scans to estimate the bite force and stress distribution of the phorusrhacid Andalgalornis.
facts.quote: A 2010 study by Degrange and colleagues of the medium-sized phorusrhacid Andalgalornis, based on finite element analysis using CT scans, estimated its bite force and stress distribution in its skull.

facts.statement: Studies found that Titanis and similar large phorusrhacids had a bite force of 133 Newtons at the bill tip and lost significant intracranial immobility.
facts.quote: They found its bite force to be 133 Newtons at the bill tip, and showed it had lost a large degree of intracranial immobility (mobility of skull bones in relation to each other), as was also the case for other large phorusrhacids such as Titanis.

facts.statement: Researchers interpreted the loss of intracranial immobility in Titanis as an adaptation for enhanced skull rigidity, showing low stress under vertical force but high stress under sideways loading.
facts.quote: These researchers interpreted this loss as an adaptation for enhanced rigidity of the skull; compared to the modern red-legged seriema and white-tailed eagle, the skull of the phorusrhacid showed relatively high stress under sideways loadings, but low stress where force was applied up and down, and in simulations of "pullback" where the head returned to its normal position.

facts.statement: A 2012 study by Claudia Tambussi and colleagues found that the neck of Andalgalornis was divided into three sections based on vertebrae morphology.
facts.quote: A 2012 follow-up study by Claudia Tambussi and colleagues analyzed the flexibility of the neck of Andalgalornis based on the morphology of its neck vertebrae, finding the neck to be divided into three sections.

facts.statement: Manual manipulation of vertebrae suggested Andalgalornis neck musculature and skeleton were adapted to carry a large head and raise it after full extension.
facts.quote: By manually manipulating the vertebrae, they concluded that the neck musculature and skeleton of Andalgalornis were adapted to carrying a large head and for raising the head after the neck had been fully extended.

facts.statement: A 2012 thesis by Degrange found that large-bodied phorusrhacids like Titanis had bite forces between 1,000 and 2,000 Newtons.
facts.quote: A 2012 thesis by Degrange found phorusrhacids to have had far greater bite forces than assumed previously, with the large-bodied taxa like Titanis having a bite force of 1,000~2,000N.

facts.statement: A 2020 study by Degrange identified two main skull morphotypes in phorusrhacids derived from a seriema-like ancestor.
facts.quote: A 2020 study of phorusrhacid skull morphology by Degrange found that there were two main morphotypes within the group, derived from a seriema-like ancestor.

facts.statement: The "Terror Bird Skull Type" included Titanis and other large members, characterized by more specialized and rigid skulls compared to the ancestral "Psilopterine Skull Type".
facts.quote: These were the "Psilopterine Skull Type", which was plesiomorphic (more similar to the ancestral type), and the "Terror Bird Skull Type", which included Titanis and other large members, that was more specialized, with more rigid skulls.

facts.statement: Although different, both skull types handled prey similarly, with the rigid "Terror Bird" skull's larger bite force adapting it for larger prey.
facts.quote: Despite the differences, studies have shown the two types handled prey similarly; the more rigid skulls and resulting larger bite force of the "Terror Bird" type would have been an adaptation to handling larger prey.

facts.statement: During the Blancan stage, Titanis lived alongside endemic mammals and new immigrants from Asia and South America.
facts.quote: During the Blancan stage, Titanis lived alongside both endemic mammals as well as new immigrants from Asia and South America.

facts.statement: Titanis inhabited tropical or subtropical climates, with traditional interpretations suggesting dense forests and varied flora.
facts.quote: The localities in which Titanis is known are all tropical or subtropical in climate, with traditional interpretations indicating a habitat of dense forests and a variety of flora.

facts.statement: Recent interpretations suggest Titanis lived in xeric thorn-scrubs and savannas within a mosaic of communities in Pliocene-Pleistocene Florida.
facts.quote: More recent interpretations suggest that the environment of Pliocene-Pleistocene Florida was a mosaic of different communities (i.e. a mixture of forests, savannas, wetlands, etc.), and that Titanis lived in areas of xeric thorn-scrubs and savannas.

facts.statement: Blancan age strata in Florida where Titanis fossils are found preserve over a hundred species of mammals.
facts.quote: The Blancan age strata of Florida from Titanis sites preserve over a hundred species and many different mammals.

facts.statement: The Blancan fauna included extinct proboscideans and perissodactyls such as grazing equids and browsing tapirs.
facts.quote: This includes extinct proboscideans and perissodactyls represented by grazing equids and browsing tapirs.

facts.statement: The Blancan fauna included a wide array of artiodactyls such as peccaries, camelids, pronghorns, and white-tailed deer.
facts.quote: A wide array of artiodactyls existed, including peccaries, camelids, pronghorns, and the extant white-tailed deer.

facts.statement: The Blancan fauna included armadillos and relatives like pampatheres, glyptodonts, and dasypodids.
facts.quote: Armadillos and their relatives are also known such as a pampathere, a glyptodont, and dasypodids.

facts.statement: Carnivorans in the Blancan fauna included borophagins, hyaenids, and saber-toothed cats.
facts.quote: The carnivorans include borophagins, hyaenids, and "saber-toothed" cats.

facts.statement: Large rodents in the Blancan fauna included capybaras and porcupines.
facts.quote: Large rodents are represented by capybaras and porcupines.

facts.statement: Fossils associated with Titanis include a variety of reptiles such as lizards, turtles, and snakes.
facts.quote: Along with mammals, a menagerie of reptiles including lizards, turtles, and snakes is known from fossils.

facts.statement: Abundant avifauna fossils associated with Titanis include birds of prey, the teratorn Teratornis, and turkeys.
facts.quote: There are abundant remains of avifauna, with thousands of known fossils, including birds of prey, the teratorn Teratornis, one of the largest flight-capable birds known, and turkeys.
